title: Customer churn prediction system: a machine learning approach
harvard_reference: Lalwani, P., Mishra, M.K., Chadha, J.S. and Sethi, P. (2022) 'Customer churn prediction system: a machine learning approach', Computing, 104(2), pp. 271-294. doi:10.1007/s00607-021-00908-y.
abstract_summary: The paper presents a six-phase pipeline for telecom customer churn prediction: data pre-processing, feature analysis, feature selection with a gravitational search algorithm (GSA), an 80/20 train/test split, model fitting (logistic regression, naive Bayes, SVM with linear and polynomial kernels, decision tree, random forest, KNN, and boosting/ensemble variants including AdaBoost, AdaBoost with extra trees, AdaBoost-wrapped random forest/SVM/logistic regression, XGBoost and CatBoost), 5-fold cross-validation on the training set for hyperparameter tuning, and evaluation on the test set with confusion-matrix metrics and AUC. The abstract reports that AdaBoost and XGBoost gave the highest accuracy (81.71% and 80.8%) and that both reached the highest AUC of 84%. The dataset is not named in the abstract, but Table 2 ('Feature vector and their types') lists the 21 fields of the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn file (customer id, gender, senior citizen, partner, dependents, tenure, phone service, multiple lines, internet service, online security, online backup, device protection, tech support, streaming TV, streaming movies, contract, paperless billing, payment method, monthly charges, total charges, churn). Table 6 ('Comparison of machine learning models', test set) gives accuracy / AUC of: logistic regression 80.45% / 82; decision tree 80.14% / 83; random forest 78.04% / 82; random forest (AdaBoost) 81.21% / 82; AdaBoost 81.71% / 84; AdaBoost (extra tree) 81.14% / 72; KNN 79.64% / 80; naive Bayes 77.07% / 80; SVM linear 79.14% / 79; SVM poly 80.21% / 80; SVM (AdaBoost) 74.07% / 80; logistic regression (AdaBoost) 76.57% / 78; XGBoost 80.8% / 84; CatBoost 81.8% / 82. Table 3 gives 5-fold CV accuracies (logistic regression 79.85, decision tree 79.56, random forest 79.28, AdaBoost 80.72, XGBoost 79.5, CatBoost 80.34, KNN 78.51, naive Bayes 75.86).

claims_supported.claim: On the IBM/Kaggle Telco Customer Churn dataset, boosting methods (AdaBoost/XGBoost) reached about 81 % accuracy, with tree ensembles and logistic regression finishing close together.
claims_supported.where: Accuracy figures: Abstract ('Adaboost and XGboost Classifier gives the highest accuracy of 81.71% and 80.8% respectively'; both AUC 84%) and Table 6 'Comparison of machine learning models' (AdaBoost 81.71%, XGBoost 80.8%, CatBoost 81.8%, random forest (AdaBoost) 81.21%, AdaBoost (extra tree) 81.14%, logistic regression 80.45%, decision tree 80.14%, plain random forest 78.04%). Dataset: Table 2 'Feature vector and their types' lists exactly the 21 fields of the Kaggle/IBM Telco Customer Churn file; the accessible portions of the paper (abstract, tables, figure captions) do not print the words 'Kaggle' or 'IBM', so the attribution rests on that field-for-field schema match plus citing works (Jagini, 2025, Stockholm University MSc thesis, Table 2.1 labels the Lalwani results 'IBM Telco Customer Churn Dataset'; a 2025 citing paper indexed by Semantic Scholar describes the study as using 'the Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 records, 21 attributes)'). 'Finishing close together' is the report's reading of Table 6, not a sentence in the paper: logistic regression (80.45%) sits within about 1.4 points of the boosted tree ensembles (80.8-81.8%), and a citing paper (Akan et al., 2022, IEEE UEMCON) summarises the conclusion as XGBoost and AdaBoost best 'with no significant difference'. Two qualifications: (i) plain random forest scored 78.04%, 2.4 points BELOW logistic regression, so the wording should be 'boosted tree ensembles' or should acknowledge random forest; (ii) CatBoost (81.8%) narrowly exceeded AdaBoost (81.71%) in Table 6, so do not describe AdaBoost/XGBoost as the single best models, only as reaching about 81%.

caveats: 1) Results come from a single 80/20 split with no confidence intervals or repeated runs; differences of about one accuracy point between logistic regression, decision tree and the boosted ensembles are within plausible sampling noise, so 'close together' should be stated as an observation, not a statistically tested finding. 2) The abstract's claim that AdaBoost and XGBoost give the highest accuracy is not exactly borne out by the paper's own Table 6, where CatBoost (81.8%) edges AdaBoost (81.71%); cite AdaBoost/XGBoost for about 81% accuracy and the joint-best AUC of 84%, not as the outright winners. 3) Plain random forest (78.04%) underperformed logistic regression; only AdaBoost-wrapped random forest (81.21%) was close to the top. 4) Accuracy on this dataset (about 26.5% churners) is a weak headline metric: a majority-class predictor scores about 73.5%; the paper's AUC figures (84% for AdaBoost/XGBoost) are the more informative comparison. 5) The 5-fold CV accuracies in Table 3 (e.g. AdaBoost 80.72%, XGBoost 79.5%) are lower than the test-set values in Table 6, so quote which table you are using. 6) Figures were obtained after gravitational-search feature selection and the paper's tuning, so they are not directly comparable to a plain scikit-learn baseline on the raw Kaggle file. 7) The words 'Kaggle' and 'IBM' were not visible in the accessible parts of the paper; the dataset identification rests on the exact schema match and citing works.
